title: How to Fact-Check AI
hook: You can't tell a true AI answer from a made-up one by reading it — both sound equally sure. So build a habit: for anything that matters, verify it somewhere that isn't the AI.
key_points: Confidence is not accuracy — a fluent answer is not a checked one.
Verify against a real source you can see: official sites, primary documents, multiple outlets.
Ask the AI for its sources, then actually open and read them.
Be most skeptical of specific facts: names, dates, numbers, quotes, citations, laws.
content_html: The hardest thing about AI errors is that they're invisible from the inside of an answer. A correct fact and a complete fabrication are written in the same calm, fluent, authoritative voice — the model doesn't know which is which, so it can't warn you. That means "it sounded right" is worthless as a test. The only reliable approach is to verify important claims outside the AI, against something you can actually see.
extra_html: A practical routine: for anything with real stakes, confirm it against a primary or official source — the actual government site, the original document, the company's own page — or check whether several independent outlets say the same thing. Ask the AI to provide its sources, but don't stop there: open them, because models sometimes invent citations, complete with realistic-looking titles and authors that don't exist. Aim your skepticism where hallucinations cluster: specific names, dates, statistics, quotes, legal rules, and medical or financial details. Conceptual explanations ("how does a mortgage work?") are usually safe to trust; specific facts ("what was the 2019 rate?") are exactly where to slow down. The goal isn't paranoia — it's a reflex to double-check the details before you act on them or pass them on.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

related.title: AI in Search
related.hook: Search engines now answer in sentences, not just links. Convenient — but the AI summary can be wrong or miss context, and the links underneath are still where the truth lives.

related.title: Using AI Responsibly
related.hook: The point of AI literacy isn't to use AI for everything — it's to use it well: check its work, be honest that you used it, and know the moments to put it down.

prereqs.title: When AI Makes Things Up
prereqs.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't you spot a hallucination just by reading the answer?

choices.text: True and made-up answers are written with the same confidence
Hallucinations are always full of typos
The AI flags wrong answers in red

flashcards.explanation_html: The model has no internal sense of certainty it shows you — a fabricated fact reads exactly as smoothly as a correct one. Only outside checking reveals it.

flashcards.prompt: What kinds of AI output deserve the most suspicion?
flashcards.back_html: Specifics: names, dates, numbers, quotes, citations, and legal or medical claims. These are exactly where models invent plausible-sounding details.

flashcards.prompt: The AI gives you a source for its claim. What next?

choices.text: Open the source and confirm it actually says that
Trust it — providing a source proves it's right
Ask the AI if the source is real

flashcards.explanation_html: Models sometimes invent citations outright. A named source means nothing until you open it and verify it exists and supports the claim.
